model.label: Tax-funded, regionally run national health service: 21 regions finance and provide most care from regional income taxes and state grants, municipalities run long-term and home care, with capped user fees

overview.statement: Health care in Sweden is part of social protection, financed mainly through taxes and mostly publicly provided; its stated goal is good health and care on equal terms, and it covers almost everyone who lives or works in the country, about 10.6 million people.

locator.section: How is the health system organized?

overview.statement: The 21 regions carry the main responsibility for financing, organising and providing health care; the 290 municipalities finance and provide care in ordinary and special housing for older people and people with functional impairments, and school health care.

Coverage rests on registered residence and there is no predefined benefits package: the Health and Medical Services Act obliges the responsible authorities to provide care to all residents according to need, and all cost-effective treatments are meant to be included.

The Commonwealth Fund profile dates the basis of today's system to the 1982 Health and Medical Services Act, which required equal access to all medical care, including prevention, for all legal residents and gave regions and municipalities full responsibility for delivering care.

locator.section: Coverage and Access: Background and History

overview.statement: All residents are entitled to publicly funded care, as are people from other EU countries who work or are registered job-seekers in Sweden, and their families; asylum seekers and undocumented migrants do not have full access but are entitled to emergency and dental care (Commonwealth Fund).

locator.section: The Role of Public Health Insurance

overview.statement: Hospital care is still dominated by public institutions, but private providers now run about 44% of primary care centres, with wide variation between regions; the expansion was accelerated by the 2010 patient choice law, which let people choose any accredited public or private provider.

Each region runs a highly integrated system in which most hospitals are owned and operated by the region, while the mix of public and private outpatient providers differs a great deal between regions.

financing.statement: Health care is funded mainly by local taxes, topped up by national government grants and user charges. In 2022 national government spending accounted for 23% of health spending, the regions for 44% and the municipalities for 19%.

Both regions and municipalities levy proportional income taxes on their residents to fund health care, supplemented by national government grants and user charges; state dental care subsidies are paid through national social insurance, whose revenue comes mainly from employer payroll fees.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: In 2026 the average regional income tax rate is 11.69% and the average municipal rate 20.69%, giving an average total local income tax rate of 32.38% (Statistics Sweden).

locator.section: Table: Total kommunal skattesats 2023-2026, genomsnitt för riket

financing.statement: The local tax rate is the sum of the municipal and regional rates and is levied on individuals' taxable earned income; the national average is weighted by each municipality's tax base (Statistics Sweden).
Regional income tax fell from 71.4% of regional revenue in 2015 to 64.4% in 2020, while the share from national government grants rose from 19.7% to 28.4%.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: General state grants are paid per inhabitant through a formula meant to equalise differences in tax base and spending needs, so that regions and municipalities can keep similar standards whatever their average income or need.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: Most of the targeted state grant to the regions, equal to 7.2% of total regional revenue, reimburses them for pharmaceuticals in the national drug benefit scheme.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: Private sources paid 14% of current health spending in 2022, 92% of it out of pocket by households; voluntary health insurance plays mainly a complementary role and accounts for about 1% of total health spending.
In 2023 public spending made up 86% of total health spending, against an EU average of 80%, and out-of-pocket payments 13%, against 16% across the EU.

Of SEK 692,835 million total health spending in 2023, central, regional and municipal government paid SEK 596,404 million, private insurance SEK 4,317 million and households SEK 89,774 million out of pocket (Commonwealth Fund).

About 10% of people aged 16-64 have voluntary health insurance, often paid for by their employer; it accounts for less than 1% of health spending, is sold by commercial insurers that decide who is eligible, generally excludes emergency, intensive, highly specialised and chronic care, and covers care by private providers.

locator.section: 2.7.1 Regulation and governance of third-party payers

financing.statement: In 2023 about 7% of the population had private health insurance, mostly group policies provided through employers and trade unions; it complements public care with non-urgent services such as preventive, planned specialist and rehabilitative care (Commonwealth Fund).
Since July 2018, health insurance paid for by an employer has been a taxable benefit for the employee.

The Swedish Tax Agency values employer-paid health insurance at the employer's cost, normally the premium; when a policy covers both taxable and tax-free services, the taxable benefit may be set at a standard 60% of the premium.

covered.statement: In 2023 public sources covered 99% of inpatient care costs, 93% of outpatient care and 42% of dental care, all above the EU averages; pharmaceuticals, at 54%, were the exception, slightly below the EU average because of graduated co-payments.

With no explicit national benefits package, the principle is to provide all necessary, cost-effective treatment according to medical need; the National Board of Health and Welfare and the association of regions (SKR) write common guidelines to limit variation among the 21 regions.

Priority setting follows an ethical platform with three principles: equal human dignity and rights, priority to those in greatest need (more severe disease before less severe), and a reasonable relation between costs and health effects when choosing between options.

Publicly covered services include preventive, primary, inpatient, outpatient, mental health, maternity, rehabilitation, long-term, home and palliative care; dental care, pharmaceuticals and assistive devices such as mobility and hearing aids are covered only partly or with subsidies (Commonwealth Fund).

locator.section: Services Covered by Public Health Insurance

covered.statement: The Dental and Pharmaceutical Benefits Agency (TLV) decides which medicines enter the national benefits scheme and sets their list prices using an ethical platform of human dignity, need and solidarity, and cost-effectiveness; there is no single explicit cost-effectiveness threshold, and willingness to pay varies with disease severity and, increasingly, with the size of the patient population.
For new hospital therapies, the regions' Council for New Therapies (NT-rådet) issues national recommendations based on TLV analyses, and the law requires local medicines committees.

cost_sharing.statement: Patient fees are modest and combined with annual caps: a primary care visit typically costs SEK 150-300 (about EUR 14-28) depending on the region, and separate annual ceilings apply to consultation fees and to prescription costs.

Fees are charged for almost all services and medical products, with exceptions including child and maternity care and many services for people aged 85 and older; the regions set the fees, so they differ across the country.
Under the outpatient high-cost protection, a patient's fees are capped at SEK 1,450 in a 12-month period, and hospital inpatient fees are capped at SEK 130 per day (Commonwealth Fund).

A July 2025 reform of medicine cost-sharing raised the annual out-of-pocket ceiling from SEK 2,900 to SEK 3,800 and made patients pay a larger share at first, with subsidies rising step by step; once a person's medicine costs reach SEK 7,117 in a year, a free card covers everything further.

From 2026, people aged 67 and over pay 10% of a set reference price for covered dental treatment of disease, pain and repairs, the state pays the other 90%, and clinics may not charge more than the reference price; check-ups and preventive care are not part of this scheme.
From 2026 the general dental care allowance is SEK 600 for patients aged 20-23 and those at or above the pension reference age (currently 67), and SEK 300 for other adults.

locator.section: Varför ingår inte undersökning och andra hälsofrämjande insatser i reformen?

cost_sharing.statement: Generic substitution is mandatory, and compliance is so high that extra co-payments by patients who choose a branded drug make up only 0.3% of the benefit scheme's costs.
Out-of-pocket health spending equalled 3.4% of household expenses in 2021, close to the OECD average of 3.3% (Commonwealth Fund).

financial_hardship.statement: Among people applying to the Enforcement Authority for debt relief, the share naming illness as the cause of their payment problems (stated by the applicant together with the case officer) fell from 19% in 2019 to 10% in 2024, while the share naming overconsumption rose from 18% to 35%.

additional_care.statement: Long-term care is comprehensive and publicly financed, with national policy favouring home care over institutions; municipalities means-test, finance and organise it, and services generally require a needs assessment, except for things such as security alarms and some home care.
Municipal long-term care services are generally means-tested on income and assets, and fees, which vary by municipality, are capped at SEK 2,350 a month (Commonwealth Fund).
In 2021 about 15.7% of people over 65 received long-term care, 77% of them in their own homes (Commonwealth Fund).

Dental care is a competitive market with public and private operators; about two thirds of adult dental care under the general allowance is delivered at around 3,550 clinics run by 2,000 private providers.

access.statement: In 2024, 3.9% of people in Sweden who reported a need for medical care could not get at least some of it, slightly above the EU average of 3.6%.
Since 2021, about 30% of patients have consistently waited longer than the 90-day legal limit for a first specialist consultation.

In 2024, 7.2% of people at risk of poverty who reported medical needs could not get at least some care, against 6.0% for the same group across the EU; the Country Health Profile says waiting delays hit lower-income groups hardest.

In a 2025 Eurofound e-survey cited by the Country Health Profile, 7.0% of people reported some unmet need for primary care and 11.0% for mental health care, both above EU averages and continuing an upward trend.

Under the national care guarantee, patients should be offered a specialist appointment or planned treatment within 90 days of referral; if the region cannot meet this, it must arrange and pay for care elsewhere (Commonwealth Fund).
In the three largest regions (Stockholm, Skåne and Västra Götaland) almost no residents live more than 45 minutes from a hospital, but in more sparsely populated regions 15-36% do.

Relatively few people forgo care because of patient fees, though doing so is clearly more common for dental care, and patient surveys show long waits are a bigger reason for forgoing care than out-of-pocket costs.

locator.section: Box 2 What are the key gaps in coverage?

access.statement: Reliance on temporary locum doctors in primary care has fallen: the number of regions depending on them to keep basic services going dropped from eight to four between 2023 and 2025, as most regions now limit such contracts for permanent posts.

outcomes.statement: In 2024 life expectancy at birth reached a record 84.1 years, the highest in the EU together with Italy.
In 2022 Sweden had the lowest avoidable mortality rate in the EU, with both treatable and preventable mortality more than a third below the EU averages.
In the GBD 2019 study, Sweden's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 90.4 (95% uncertainty interval 88.4-92.1) in 2019, 14.0 points higher than in 1990.

locator.table: Table: HAQ Index estimates by location; row values in order: 2019 overall (0-74 years), young (0-14), working (15-64), post-working (65-74), then absolute change 1990-2019 for the same four groups

outcomes.statement: In 2023, 83% of invited women took part in breast cancer screening, against an EU average of 57.5%, and cervical screening participation reached 78%, more than a third above the EU average.
In 2023 the combined hospital admission rate for diabetes, congestive heart failure, asthma and COPD was 25% below the EU average.
HPV vaccination coverage among 15-year-old girls rose from 76% in 2018 to 86% in 2024, second in the EU and about 35% above the EU average.

Treatable mortality is higher among people with less education, and the gap between the regions with the lowest and highest rates is about 20 deaths per 100,000; differences by education and region have narrowed since 2013.

costs.statement: Health spending was the fourth highest in the EU in 2023 at EUR 4,688 per person (adjusted for purchasing power), about one fifth above the EU average.
From 2015 to 2023, real health spending per person grew by 0.9% a year on average, as a 1.2% annual rise in public spending outweighed a 1.0% annual fall in private spending.
In 2023 outpatient services took 33% of total health spending, one of the highest shares among higher-spending EU countries, while inpatient care took only 22% against an EU average of 28%.
Long-term care made up 28% of total health spending in 2023, compared with an EU average of 18%.
Retail pharmaceutical spending was EUR 454 per person in 2023, 11% below the EU average of EUR 510, even though total health spending per person was 22% above the EU average.
A 2023 TLV comparison found Sweden had the lowest prices among 20 European countries for medicines facing generic competition.
Confidential rebates from manufacturers are growing: paybacks were estimated at SEK 3.3 billion in 2023 and are projected to reach SEK 4.7 billion in 2026.

Compared with countries with similar treatable mortality, Sweden spends more on health; it does well on technical efficiency measures such as length of hospital stay, day-case surgery and generic substitution, but less well on staff turnover, sickness absence and staff deployment.

In a study of 2016 data from the four largest regions, expected lifetime health care spending was 17.9% higher for women and 16.8% higher for men in the lowest income fifth than in the highest, despite their shorter lives.
In 1980 US health spending was comparable to Sweden's and Germany's, at 8.2% of GDP; since then the US has far outpaced the other nine countries in Mirror, Mirror 2024.

what_works.statement: The Country Health Profile credits the larger role of nurses in Swedish primary care, especially in managing diabetes and asthma, as a key driver of the sustained fall in hospital admissions for chronic conditions.
Antibiotic use is the second lowest in the EU: an estimated 10.9 defined daily doses per 1,000 people in 2023, 45% below the EU average and already within Sweden's 2030 reduction target.
Since a 2020 pilot, Sweden has paid manufacturers of critical antibiotics fixed annual sums instead of paying by sales volume, which secures supply without rewarding overuse.

According to the industry's EFPIA W.A.I.T. indicator, 50% of medicines approved in the EU in 2020-2023 reached Swedish patients (EU average 46%), and the median time from EU authorisation to public availability was about 361 days, against 578 days on average in the EU.

Since 2015 all regions have used a joint model with authorities and companies to negotiate prices and manage the introduction of certain new drugs on the Council on New Therapies' recommendations; in 2021 these agreements saved an estimated SEK 2.7 billion on prescription drugs.

locator.section: Box 8 Is there waste in pharmaceutical spending?

what_works.statement: After the out-of-pocket fee for mammography screening was removed in 2016, attendance rose most among the women least likely to attend: from 62.9% to 65.8% among non-Nordic women with the lowest income, and from 59.2% to 62.0% among women with four or more risk factors for non-attendance (14 of 21 regions, 2014-2015 vs 2017-2018).
Hospital patients report good experiences in international comparison: in 2021, 92% felt involved in decisions about their care and 94% said doctors often or always treated them professionally.

locator.section: Box 6 What do patients think of the care they receive?

what_works.statement: Capital spending on health information technology reached EUR 5.9 million per 100,000 people in 2023, the third highest in the EU after Austria and Denmark and more than two and a half times the EU average.

problems.statement: In 2023 Sweden had the fewest hospital beds in the EU, 1.9 per 1,000 people against an EU average of 5.1.

Despite extra funding to staff new beds, the National Board of Health and Welfare recorded 40 fewer staffed beds in 2024 than in 2023, and its data point to a shortage of nursing staff, rather than of physical capacity or money, as the root cause of the bed shortfall.
The goal of closing the hospital bed gap by 2026 has been pushed back to 2027, and the National Board of Health and Welfare warns that without stronger action balance may not be reached before 2033.
Between 2021 and 2024, around 45% of patients waited longer than the 90-day statutory guarantee for elective surgery.
Between August 2023 and August 2024, 41% of cataract patients nationally waited longer than 90 days, ranging from 7% in Stockholm to 70% in Västerbotten.
In 2022 there were an estimated 40% fewer full-time-equivalent GPs than primary care centres said they needed.

locator.section: Box 3 What are the key strengths and weaknesses of primary care?

problems.statement: All 21 regions report shortages of both general practitioners and specialist doctors, with the biggest gaps in rural and northern areas.
General practitioners make up only 14% of the physician workforce, against an EU average of 20%.

Fewer Swedish patients experience primary care as person-centred, they are less satisfied with care coordination than other Europeans, and availability of care and outcomes vary without justification between socioeconomic groups and regions.

Demand for voluntary insurance may reflect long waits for public care; because people with such insurance get care faster on average but are unlikely to have greater medical needs, this sits uneasily with the legal principle of care on equal terms and according to need.
The 2015 Patient Act's nationwide free choice of primary and outpatient specialist care had unexpected effects: new private digital care providers and higher spending.

Hospital technical efficiency is weaker than in other countries, partly because nurse specialists are hard to recruit and keep, and hospital productivity is slightly below Denmark, Norway and Finland.

reforms.statement: In 2018 Sweden began a major reform, Good quality, local health care (God och nära vård), backed by substantial state funding, to move care from hospitals to accessible, person-centred local care through closer work between primary care, outpatient specialist services and municipal care.

The 2025 state budget gave SEK 3.7 billion to primary and local specialist care under God och nära vård, SEK 1 billion to cut surgical waiting lists and another SEK 1 billion shared among the regions according to performance indicators.

A 2024 government inquiry proposed one-off, performance-based state payments, shorter time limits and earlier referral to other regions to strengthen the care guarantee; on that basis the National Board of Health and Welfare was told to distribute SEK 497 million in 2025, linked to extra hip replacements, pelvic organ prolapse repairs and cataract operations.

A government committee asked to prepare a full or partial state takeover of health care reported in June 2025; it did not propose a takeover but more state steering of workforce supply, medicines, vaccination, screening, forensic psychiatry and air ambulances.
In August 2026 the government appointed an inquiry to propose national principles for which health services must be available throughout Sweden.

Because the current law stresses the regions' duty to provide care more than the patient's right to receive it, the 2026 inquiry must also propose a stronger care guarantee; its final report is due by 15 February 2028.

The first stage of a dental reform, planned to start on 1 January 2026, strengthens high-cost protection for people aged 67 and over; to pay for it the age limit for free child and youth dental care was cut from 23 to 19 and for state dental support from 24 to 20, and the government plans about SEK 3.4 billion a year from 2026.
The government's change to the medicine high-cost protection thresholds is expected to cut public spending on retail medicines by about SEK 2 billion a year from 2026.

A 2021 reform of medical education replaced the internship with a six-year programme leading directly to a licence, followed by a year of basic training (Bastjänstgöring) and then residency of at least five years.

The 2018 Care Coordination Act set a three-day limit for moving patients ready for discharge out of hospital, requires hospitals to notify primary and social care earlier, and fines municipalities that do not meet the requirements (Commonwealth Fund).

us_lessons.statement: A 2024 narrative review comparing private health insurance in the United States and Sweden concluded that the US might benefit from wider access to public health insurance, particularly when families face unemployment.
